production.text: A glazed stoneware vessel and commissioned paintings belong to different forms of skilled making.

participation.text: Court artists and scholar-artists could give painting different social purposes.

obligation.text: A fiscal proposal would connect reserves, household seasonal need and tax collection. Its language of benefit needs testing against actual borrowing, repayment and official practice.

name: Song worlds: a bowl and competing ideals
place: China; Northern capital at Kaifeng, later southern court
geographicPrecision: Kaifeng locator for the northern phase; the bowl’s Jian ware attribution is a different place of production.

interval.label: Song dynastic frame, 960–1279 CE
interval.note: Northern Song 960–1127; Southern Song1127–1279. Simultaneous Liao and Jin states are distinct, not erased by this frame.

question: Can objects and paintings embody competing views of an ordered world?
summary: Song institutions joined court service, commercial activity and skilled production. A tea bowl makes material work visible; a proposal about crop loans exposes a different relationship between officials and farming households. Neither stands for everyone’s experience. Northern and Southern Song had different capital settings, while neighboring states and changing borders prevent a single unchanging picture of China.

sections.title: A bowl begins with work, rather than a dynasty label
sections.text: This Jian-ware bowl is stoneware with a dark, streaked glaze conventionally called hare’s fur. Its catalogue date is the eleventh–twelfth century, a range spanning more than one political phase. Forming a vessel and controlling its fired surface required practical skill. The photograph shows a finished object; it does not identify its potter, fuel supply, purchaser or a shipment to the capital. A name for a ware is not a complete workshop history.

citations.locator: Artwork details, accession 91.1.226 and supplied image

sections.title: Market exchange depended on other people’s tasks
sections.text: The Columbia teaching account describes markets spreading through cities and the countryside, specialized producers and water transport for bulky goods such as grain. Growing for sale linked a household’s choices to buyers and prices. Boats still needed loading, routes and provisioning. Commercial activity therefore involved several kinds of work, beyond making a fine bowl. The presence of markets does not by itself establish that every cultivator became wealthier or had equal bargaining power.

citations.locator: Robert Hymes excerpt; grain transport and cash-cropping passages

sections.title: A proposal tried to alter the timing of debt
sections.text: In the 1069 crop-loan memorial, the fiscal commission proposed using public reserves to lend before harvest and accept repayment with later tax instalments. It also described buying grain when prices were low and selling when high to moderate price swings. For a household, receiving resources before a crop was ready could matter as much as an annual total. This is the policy’s stated rationale. Whether officials made borrowing voluntary, and how repayment worked after poor harvests, require evidence beyond the proposal.

citations.locator: Longer selection: 1069 memorial, reserves, loans and repayment

sections.title: Court culture did not exhaust government
sections.text: The Met essay contrasts imperial painting patronage with scholar-official expression. Such cultural differences help explain competing ideals, but offices also collected taxes, kept records and provisioned military forces. Hartman argues that accounts focused only on elite literati leave other political workers out. Read the bowl, a court ideal and a fiscal proposal together without making them interchangeable evidence. A ceramic surface cannot tell us whether a named loan was repaid.

citations.locator: Introduction pp. 3–5: political actors and fiscal/military work

sections.title: The southern court belongs to a later phase
sections.text: The conventional Northern Song frame ends in 1127, when the court lost its northern capital to the Jurchen Jin. Southern Song government was centered at Hangzhou; it ended with the Mongol conquest in 1279. These transitions changed political geography. They did not make a bowl’s broad date exact or turn the whole region into one uninterrupted jurisdiction.

deeperReading.title: Follow a reserve through the proposed cycle
deeperReading.text: The memorial joins three things often separated in a summary: grain stocks, cash and the timing of tax collection. Loans used reserves to address a seasonal shortage, then brought repayment into an official collection cycle. It also allowed delay after disaster. The diagram maps these proposed relationships, not a measured flow of grain or money. A government’s justification explains why its authors wanted a measure adopted. Local accounts, petitions and disputes would test what a particular household actually faced.

citations.locator: Longer selection: kinds of reserves, tax instalments and disaster deferral

deeperReading.title: A capital move does not date a ceramic
deeperReading.text: Keep the dynasty’s phase labels separate from the object’s range. The catalogue’s eleventh–twelfth-century description remains useful even without assigning the bowl to one side of 1127. Kaifeng and Hangzhou are approximate capital-area locators; neither point is the bowl’s documented findspot or production kiln. Nor does selecting a year on the atlas narrow the museum’s date. This distinction allows a material investigation to sit within a longer political account without supplying missing provenance.

deeperReading.title: Who appears in a history of government?
deeperReading.text: Hartman’s introduction reviews sharply different modern interpretations of Song governance. His own argument broadens attention to clerks and military officials, as well as the monarch and literati. This is an interpretive intervention, not a settled vote among historians. It prompts a practical question: whose work disappears when the surviving voices belong mostly to highly educated officials? A household budget or a clerk’s register could answer questions that a painting or policy defense leaves open.

citations.locator: Introduction pp. 1–5: contending interpretations and political participation

evidenceReading.title: Distinguish a proposal, an object and an interpretation
evidenceReading.introduction: The sources do different jobs. None supplies a census of ordinary experience.

items.label: A seasonal policy
items.text: The 1069 memorial proposes lending before harvest and repayment with later tax collections.
items.interpretation: This explains intended timing, not the observed debt or consent of every household.

items.label: A finished surface
items.text: The Met identifies stoneware with hare’s-fur glaze and an eleventh–twelfth-century range.
items.interpretation: Material and date attribution do not identify the maker, buyer or loan used to make it.

items.label: A modern historical argument
items.text: Hartman challenges a political history limited to emperor and literati.
items.interpretation: An attributed interpretation helps frame questions without becoming a contemporary Song witness.

steps: Trace the diagram from reserves to a household before harvest.

review.scope: Bounded C6 account with main/deeper/evidence reading, family entry, phased context, sourced place study and inspected/modern media.
limitations: No local crop-loan registers, household budgets, original Chinese consultation or independent assessment of implementation.
The bowl’s maker, kiln, customer and journey remain unknown. The Met chronology’s erroneous Huizong/Mongol sentence is not adopted; its Jurchen/Jin entry supplies the distinct 1127 phase.
Wider rural, gender, military and neighboring-state histories remain selective.

placeStudy.title: Two Song capital areas, separate from a bowl’s provenance
placeStudy.description: Approximate modern city-area locators distinguish northern and southern court settings. They are not the bowl’s findspot, kiln or itinerary. No historical boundary or ceramic shipment is traced.

points.label: Kaifeng / Bianliang — northern capital area
points.text: The Northern Song capital before the 1127 loss to Jurchen Jin. A city-area point does not locate a particular office or the selected bowl.

points.label: Hangzhou — southern capital area
points.text: Southern Song court setting after the northern loss. The modern generalized coast is orientation, not a reconstructed twelfth-century shoreline.
